content: Puerarin, a type of herbal medicine, is commonly used in China for the treatment of ischaemic stroke. The purpose of this review was to evaluate the effects of puerarin in individuals who have experienced an ischaemic stroke. To gather relevant studies, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Stroke Group Trials Register, the Chinese Stroke Trials Register, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, EMBASE, AMED, and the China Biological Medicine Database. The search covered studies published up to August 2015. Additional efforts were made to identify further studies by reviewing reference lists, clinical trial registries, and contacting pharmaceutical companies and researchers. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) or quasi-randomized controlled trials that compared puerarin with either a placebo or no treatment in individuals with ischaemic stroke. Two independent reviewers assessed the eligibility of studies, evaluated the quality of the trials, and extracted the relevant data. A total of 20 RCTs involving 1574 participants were included in this updated review. All of these trials were published in Chinese-language journals. Fourteen of these trials had been excluded in a previous version of the review but were included in this update due to the addition of a new outcome measure. The time window for randomization of participants ranged from 4.5 hours to 10 days after the onset of stroke symptoms. In 18 of the trials, the diagnosis of ischaemic stroke was confirmed using either computed tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). A meta-analysis of two trials, which included 164 participants, found that puerarin treatment did not significantly reduce the risk of death or dependency at the final follow-up (relative risk [RR] 0.79, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.45 to 1.36). One trial with 83 participants reported that the mean Barthel Index score, a measure of functional independence, was lower in the puerarin group compared to the control group. However, a meta-analysis of 16 trials involving 1305 participants showed that puerarin reduced the proportion of participants who did not experience improvement in neurological deficits by the end of follow-up (RR 0.42, 95% CI 0.33 to 0.55). None of the included trials reported any serious adverse effects associated with puerarin. However, the overall quality of the evidence was deemed low due to incomplete reporting of study methods and the short duration of follow-up in the included trials. In conclusion, there is insufficient evidence to determine whether puerarin has a beneficial effect on survival or dependency in individuals with ischaemic stroke. High-quality, large-scale randomized controlled trials with long-term follow-up are necessary to better assess the efficacy and safety of puerarin in this population.
